_purpose: Sample user queries for the /chat harness, derived directly from the real cybersierra CLI's manifest (cybersierra manifest --raw), not invented independently. Each single_command_query maps to exactly one manifest command; composite_queries require the Planner to chain 2+ commands per skills/cyber-sierra/_internal/planner/references/planning-rules.md; adversarial_queries have no matching manifest command and should be rejected, per that same file's 'No hallucinated commands' rule. Read-only (safe:true) commands only -- write/safe:false commands were removed on purpose (see dataset/README.md 'Write operations were removed') so running this dataset never creates, sends, submits, or updates real data in whatever cybersierra backend it's pointed at. See dataset/README.md for how this was generated and how to use it.

generated_from.note: The manifest changed between this repo's initial build and this dataset's capture (notifications module and several tprm resources -- activity-logs, assessee-scans, assessee-tenant-users -- were added by a self-update in between). This dataset is a snapshot; see verify/validate_query_dataset.py for drift detection against whatever manifest is live when you run it.

composite_queries.example_query: Give me a quick compliance snapshot: how many vendors do we have, and what's on the risk dashboard?
composite_queries.notes: No data dependency between the two steps -- tests that the Planner can produce two independent, parallel-eligible (but still linearly executed, per execution-plan-schema.md's 'strictly linear') steps from one request.

composite_queries.example_query: Who am I, and how many unread notifications do I have?
List our vendors, then show me the full details of the first one.
composite_queries.notes: Step 2's id argument should be a {{step[1].*}} reference into step 1's list output -- the canonical case execution-plan-schema.md's Reference Syntax exists for.

composite_queries.example_query: Find the assessments we've sent to vendor 118898 and compare the two most recent ones.
composite_queries.notes: Step 2's ids argument depends on step 1's results ({{step[1].*}}), and also requires the model to do non-plan reasoning (picking 'the two most recent') on the returned data -- planning-rules.md is explicit that analysis like this is the agent's job post-execution, not a plan step.

composite_queries.example_query: Show me my identity, then list the user groups in my tenant.
List our draft assessees and also tell me the total assessee count, so I know how many are still in draft.
What assessment templates exist, and show me the full detail of the SOC 2 one.
composite_queries.notes: Step 2's id must be resolved from step 1's list by matching on name/description -- there's no direct 'get by name' command, so this also tests whether the Planner correctly treats the SOC 2 template's id as a {{step[1].*}} reference rather than inventing an id.

composite_queries.example_query: What filter options are available for activity logs on assessee 118898, and then show me its actual activity log?
Show me my most overdue assessment, its full detail, and whether all its questions have been verified.
composite_queries.notes: A genuine 3-step chain, not just 2 -- the assessment id resolved from step 1's list is reused as {{step[1].*}} by both step 2 and step 3. This is the 'what assessments are there -> what does it do -> what's the status' flow a real vendor-risk user actually follows, expressed as three real manifest calls instead of one.

composite_queries.example_query: Pull up our most recently sent assessment, show me its full detail, and list any comments on it.
composite_queries.notes: Same 3-step shape as composite-overdue-with-verification but a different pair of dependent steps off the same step-1 id, so the Planner is tested on picking the right two follow-up commands, not just chaining any two.

composite_queries.example_query: Find our newest vendor, check whether they have any security scans, and see what's been said in their comments.
composite_queries.notes: 3-step chain rooted in tprm assessees list rather than assessments list -- step 2 and step 3 both take the assessee id resolved from step 1 ({{step[1].*}}), the same reused-id shape but on the assessee resource instead of the assessment resource.

composite_queries.example_query: Who am I, what permission policies apply to me, and what user groups exist in my tenant?
composite_queries.notes: 3-step chain where step 2's subject argument resolves from step 1's own identity ({{step[1].*}}), not from a listed record's id -- a different reference shape than the list-then-detail composites above. Step 3 has no data dependency on either prior step.

composite_queries.example_query: List our vendors and show me who's on the team for the very first one.
Show me the version history for our vendors, and give me the full profile of whichever one changed most recently.
composite_queries.notes: Step 2's id must be picked out of step 1's version history by recency, not just taken as 'the first row' -- similar non-plan reasoning requirement to composite-compare-recent's 'two most recent' pick.

adversarial_queries.example_query: Email the latest vendor risk report to our CFO.
adversarial_queries.reason: No email/report-delivery command exists anywhere in the manifest. Per planning-rules.md's rejection criteria, this should be rejected outright, not approximated with a partial plan.

adversarial_queries.example_query: Delete vendor 118898 entirely from our system.
adversarial_queries.reason: tprm assessees only has create/get/list/count/comments -- no delete action exists in the manifest at all.

adversarial_queries.example_query: Auto-approve every pending assessment without me reviewing them.
adversarial_queries.reason: No bulk-approve action exists, and this also requires conditional/branching logic ('every pending one') that planning-rules.md's Hard Rules explicitly forbid ('No branching. Plans are linear sequences.').

adversarial_queries.example_query: What's the weather like in Bangalore today?
adversarial_queries.reason: Completely outside the cybersierra domain -- no module in the manifest is even plausibly relevant. Correct behavior is answering from general knowledge or declining, never attempting a cybersierra command.

adversarial_queries.example_query: Set up a recurring monthly vendor risk report emailed to the board.
adversarial_queries.reason: No scheduling, reporting-generation, or email capability exists in the manifest. Also implicitly asks for ongoing/background behavior this one-shot CLI-driven pipeline has no mechanism for.

auth_scenarios.example_query: How many vendors do we have in total?
auth_scenarios.notes: Proves per-user access_token forwarding (CYBERSIERRA_INJECT_ACCESS_TOKEN, MORPHEUS_TOKEN injection -- see poc-wiki/v2/auth-flow.md) actually produces a real, correct answer under a real identity, not just that the harness runs at all. The access_token placeholder here is auto-resolved at runtime by eval/shared/eval_identity.py IF EVAL_MORPHEUS_EMAIL/PASSWORD/ORG/CYBERSIERRA_BASE_URL are configured (a dedicated eval tenant) -- no manual editing needed in that case. Without that configured, this scenario keeps the literal placeholder string and will fail like the invalid-token case below, same as before.

auth_scenarios.example_query: How many vendors do we have in total?
auth_scenarios.notes: Deliberately garbage token -- no real credential needed, safe to run as-is. The command still gets invoked (the real backend rejects the token, not the harness), so expected_commands is unchanged from the valid case; what's scored differently is the final answer text, via eval/local/scoring.py's check_no_internal_leakage: must read as a plain-language 'sign in again' message, must never name MORPHEUS_TOKEN/cybersierra/internal env vars -- see poc-wiki/v2/auth-flow.md's 'The model can never itself touch auth' section.
